meta.title: Irish B2 Upper Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Irish → English (see the Irish, recall the meaning) and English → Irish (see an English meaning, recall the Irish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words of Irish (Gaeilge) for an upper-intermediate learner, aligned to B2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main ideas of complex text on both concrete and abstract topics, including technical discussions in his/her field of specialisation' — a learner here is able to interact with a degree of fluency and spontaneity that makes regular interaction with native speakers quite possible without strain for either party, and to produce clear, detailed text on a wide range of subjects and explain a viewpoint on a topical issue giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Irish has a graded examination at these levels — the Teastas Eorpach na Gaeilge (TEG) of Maynooth University — whose syllabuses describe each level but do not publish a complete word list, so this deck is not an examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 131 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — the economy and work, politics and the state, law and justice, science and technology, the environment and resources, health and society, media and communication, culture and society, the abstract nouns of discussion, the verbs of arguing and reasoning, describing and evaluating, and the connectors of formal Irish — and the other 1369 are the commonest remaining words of written Irish, counted over the articles of the Irish-language Wikipedia by the WHOLE word: every form of a noun or a verb added together, and every spelling its initial mutations give it (bean, bhean, mbean). No subtitle frequency list exists for Irish, and an encyclopaedia's commonest words lean towards history, places and people, which is why the deck leads with the hand-written vocabulary. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. The 1065 nouns carry their gender, which decides how the article changes them (an fear, an bhean), and show the noun with the article, its genitive and its plural (an teach, tí, tithe); the 160 verbs are headed by the imperative, the form Irish dictionaries list a verb by (déan, "do"), and show their present, past, future and verbal noun (déanann, rinne, déanfaidh, déanamh). Behind the All forms fold a verb's tenses go by person, a noun shows its lenited and eclipsed forms (theach, dteach) and a preposition its forms with a pronoun (liom, leat, leis). The spelling is the Official Standard (An Caighdeán Oifigiúil) as Wiktionary gives it. Real example sentences come with 142 of the 1500 words, three apiece for 16 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword; few devices have an Irish voice, so the speaker may be silent. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Irish Wikipedia (ga.wikipedia.org), its articles as of 1 November 2026, counted for this deck (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
